title: Race & the Reading of Black Male Bodies
hook: The same broad-shouldered walk is read as confident in one man and threatening in another, and the difference is often in the reader's eyes, not the walker's.
why:
This book has argued from the start that reading people is an act of inference, and that inference is shaped by what the reader brings. Nowhere is that clearer, or more consequential, than in how Black men's bodies are read. A neutral face, a firm stride, a raised voice or simply a large frame can be read very differently depending on the race of the man displaying it, and research shows those differences are fast, automatic and widespread.

The chapter on the ethics of reading people in Part VI described how bias lives inside the act of looking, and the chapter on the glass ceiling in Part IV touched on how Black men's authority is received. This chapter takes up the subject fully. It covers what research has found about how Black men and boys are perceived in size, age and threat, what that means for anyone who wants to read people accurately, how Black men experience being read, and the rich nonverbal culture that often gets misread along the way.

The aim is not guilt. It is accuracy. A reader who does not know where his fast impressions go wrong will keep acting on them, and in some settings, from a shop floor to a police stop, the cost of a wrong reading falls heavily on someone else.

teach.p:
Part VI described a study in which people watched faces slowly change from angry to neutral, and judged anger to last longer on Black faces than on white ones. Nobody had told them what to see. The bias was in the perception itself, before any conscious judgment.

This is the central problem of this chapter. Most people who read Black men's bodies unfairly do not intend to, and would be dismayed to learn they do. The readings arrive fast, feel like perception rather than judgment, and are reinforced by what people expect to see. A tall Black man standing still in a shop doorway, a group of Black teenagers laughing loudly on a bus, a Black colleague who speaks forcefully in a meeting: the same behaviour from someone else might pass without notice.

For a reader of people, this means that some of the signals you think you are picking up are being supplied by you. The method of this book, a baseline, several signals rather than one, alternative explanations, and a willingness to test a reading against what actually happens, is the main defence. So is the swap test from Part IV's chapter on the glass ceiling: would you read the same behaviour the same way from a man of a different race?

The figure here stands tall and at ease, hands loose, face neutral. There is nothing in his posture that signals anything but rest. What a viewer sees in it depends, as the next blocks show, partly on him and partly on the viewer.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if people read the same behaviour in the same way regardless of the race of the man displaying it. The studies in this chapter consistently find that they do not.

teach.p:
In 2017 John Paul Wilson, Kurt Hugenberg and Nicholas Rule published seven studies with more than 950 participants in the United States. Participants saw photographs of young Black and white men and judged their height, weight, strength and how capable they would be of causing harm in a fight. The photographed men were matched for actual size.

Participants consistently judged the Black men to be larger, stronger and more capable of harm than white men of the same size. The bias was strongest for men with darker skin and more stereotypically Black facial features, even though those men were no larger. And the inflated judgments of size and strength predicted how justified participants thought it would be to use force against the men if they were suspected of a crime.

The authors were careful not to claim that this bias causes police shootings. But they argued that it could contribute: if Black men are seen as physically more threatening than they are, force against them will seem more justified than it is.

For an ordinary reader, the lesson is to distrust your sense of how big, strong or intimidating a Black man is, especially when that sense is shaping how you behave toward him. If you notice yourself feeling physically wary of a Black man who is doing nothing threatening, ask what you would feel about a white man of the same size in the same place. The figure here is tall and broad. Whether he seems imposing or simply tall is, in part, a fact about the observer.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if Black men were judged no larger or stronger than white men of the same size. Wilson and colleagues found they were judged larger, stronger and more capable of harm, and that this predicted support for using force.
teach.pullQuote: Whether a man seems imposing or simply tall is, in part, a fact about the observer.

teach.p:
The same pattern appears with children. In 2014 Phillip Atiba Goff and his colleagues asked university students to estimate the ages of boys suspected of crimes, shown in photographs. The students overestimated the ages of Black boys by an average of four and a half years, far more than for white or Latino boys. They also judged Black boys to be less innocent than other boys from about the age of ten.

The researchers also studied police officers. Officers who more strongly associated Black people with apes, on an implicit test, had used force more often against Black children in custody. The researchers noted that the direction could run either way, but the link was concerning.

An overestimate of four and a half years means a Black boy of thirteen may be seen as an adult. That changes how his behaviour is read: a teenager's boisterous play becomes a young man's aggression, a child's mistake becomes a man's choice. It also means that the protection people instinctively extend to children, the benefit of the doubt, the assumption of innocence, is withdrawn earlier from Black boys than from others.

For anyone who works with or around children, as a teacher, coach, shop worker or parent, this is worth holding onto. When a Black boy's behaviour seems threatening or deliberate, check his age, and ask how you would read the same behaviour from a white boy of that age. The figures here show a father kneeling to talk to his young son. To his father he is plainly a child. Research suggests others may not see him that way for long.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if Black boys' ages were estimated as accurately as other boys'. Goff and colleagues found an average overestimate of four and a half years, and judgments of reduced innocence from about the age of ten.

teach.p:
Bias in reading threat can operate in fractions of a second. In 2001 Keith Payne showed participants a face, either Black or white, followed immediately by a picture of either a gun or a hand tool, and asked them to identify the object as quickly as possible. When they had to respond fast, participants mistook tools for guns more often after seeing a Black face.

Payne's analysis suggested that the bias lay in the automatic part of the response, the part that operates before deliberate control can step in. Other laboratories found similar effects, including in simulations where participants decided whether to shoot armed or unarmed men on a screen.

The connection to body language is direct. A hand moving toward a pocket, a quick turn, an object held in the hand, a raised voice: each of these is read in a fraction of a second, and the reading is influenced by the race of the person. Combined with the earlier findings on size and age, the picture is of a man whose ordinary movements are more likely to be read as dangerous, by people who would sincerely deny any prejudice.

The only remedy within an individual's control is to slow down where you can, and to check fast readings against what is actually happening. That is the whole method of this book applied where it matters most. The figure here meets the viewer's gaze directly, face neutral. Research suggests that, on a Black man, a neutral face is more likely to be seen as hostile.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if race had no effect on fast judgments of threat. Payne found that tools were more often mistaken for guns after Black faces under time pressure, an effect other laboratories replicated.

teach.p:
What can an individual reader do with all this? The biases described above are fast and largely automatic, and no one becomes free of them by deciding to. But their effects on behaviour can be reduced.

First, notice the moments where they are most likely to operate. They are strongest under time pressure, in ambiguous situations, when you are tired or stressed, and when the man involved is a stranger. Those are the moments to slow down before acting on a reading.

Second, use the swap test. When you find yourself reading a Black man as aggressive, intimidating, hostile or suspicious, imagine the same behaviour, words and size from a white man. If your reading changes, look again at what actually happened. When others describe a Black colleague as aggressive or as having an attitude, ask what specifically he said and did.

Third, look for evidence that would disconfirm your reading, as every chapter of this book has asked. A man you read as intimidating who then holds a door, jokes with a cashier and walks away has given you information. Let it update your reading rather than explaining it away. Fourth, act on behaviour, not on unease. Following a man around a shop, crossing the street to avoid him, calling security because he seems out of place: each acts on a feeling rather than on anything he did. The figure here listens attentively, the posture of a reader who is taking in what someone does before deciding what he means.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if deliberate strategies such as slowing down and comparing readings had no effect on biased behaviour. They do not remove automatic bias, but they give a slower, more accurate judgment a chance to correct a fast one.

teach.p:
For Black men, all of this is not an abstract finding but a daily experience. Many describe a constant awareness of how their bodies are being read: in shops, on the street, at work, by police. Many grew up with a version of what is often called the talk, given by parents to sons: keep your hands visible, do not make sudden movements, do not argue with police, do not run, do not put your hands in your pockets in a shop.

The result is a form of the vigilance described in the previous chapter, and often of the masking described earlier in this part. Some men soften their presence deliberately: smiling more, speaking more quietly, dressing more formally, whistling as they walk at night so that others can hear they are relaxed. Part IV's chapter on the glass ceiling described research suggesting that Black chief executives with more babyish, less threatening faces were more likely to reach the top. A later chapter in this part looks at code-switching, the wider practice of adjusting the body to fit a setting.

This is not advice. It is description. Black men should not have to make themselves smaller to be read accurately, and this book does not suggest that they should. The burden of accuracy belongs with the reader.

But it is worth knowing that the relaxed, smiling, softly spoken Black colleague may be doing work you cannot see, and paying a cost for it. The figure here stands open, palms turned slightly forward. For many Black men this is not a posture but a precaution.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if Black men rarely adjusted their bodies in response to how they expected to be read. Their own accounts, and the widespread practice of the talk, describe such adjustments as common.

teach.p:
It would be a mistake to discuss Black men's body language only as something that is misread. It is also a rich dialect in its own right.

Part III described the history of the dap, the elaborate handshake that grew among Black soldiers in the Vietnam War as a gesture of solidarity and spread into everyday greeting. Greetings among many Black men are expressive and physical: the dap, the shoulder bump, the pull-in hug, the call across a room. Conversation may be more animated, with overlapping speech, raised voices and broad gestures that signal engagement and warmth rather than conflict. Within many Black communities, these are read accurately as affection and energy.

Misreading happens when outsiders apply a quieter baseline. An animated exchange is taken as an argument. A loud greeting is taken as aggression. A group of young Black men talking and laughing is taken as a threat. The behaviour is the same; the reader's map is wrong.

The remedy is the one this book recommends for every dialect: learn the baseline before you read the change. If you are invited into these greetings, match the offer as Part III advised, without awkward imitation. If you are not, simply read the warmth for what it is. The figures here bump fists, a greeting that travelled from Black American culture into everyday use across the world, and that still carries its original sense of solidarity.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if animated conversation and expressive greetings among Black men usually signalled conflict. Within the communities that use them, they are generally read as warmth and engagement, and misreading comes from outsiders applying a different baseline.

poseGallery.doCaption: Running the swap test, then listening
poseGallery.dontCaption: Reading his neutral face as attitude
poseGallery.annotation: A neutral face on a Black man is more often read as hostile. Ask what you would see in the same face on someone else.

poseGallery.doCaption: Letting him shop like anyone else
poseGallery.annotation: Acting on unease rather than behaviour is how bias becomes harm. Act on what someone does, not on how they make you feel.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Stepping out of the lift as he walks in
poseGallery.annotation: Small avoidances are noticed every time. Staying put costs nothing and tells him he was read as a person.

poseGallery.doCaption: Carrying on as you would with anyone
poseGallery.annotation: Every glance back is noticed. If his behaviour would not worry you in anyone else, let it pass.

poseGallery.doCaption: Old friends, read as old friends
poseGallery.dontCaption: Alarmed at a loud greeting across the street
poseGallery.annotation: An expressive greeting is a dialect, not a fight. Look for the laughter and the open arms before you read conflict.

caseStudy:
Neil, forty-four, manages a distribution warehouse. Within a month of promoting Desmond, a tall, quiet Black man, to shift supervisor, Neil had received two informal complaints from staff that Desmond was intimidating and had an attitude. Neil had felt a flicker of the same himself: Desmond rarely smiled in meetings and spoke bluntly.

Before acting, Neil asked both complainants what Desmond had actually said or done. Neither could name anything beyond his size, his serious face and one occasion when he had told a team to stop chatting and finish loading. Neil then thought about Alan, another supervisor, white, just as tall, who regularly told teams to hurry up in far stronger language. Nobody had ever called Alan intimidating.

Neil spoke to the two staff members, calmly, about the difference between how someone seems and what they do. He also spoke to Desmond, carefully, to check that he was getting the support he needed in the new role. Desmond was guarded at first. Then he said that he had spent his whole working life being described as intimidating, that he kept his voice low and his hands visible without thinking about it, and that he had been waiting for this conversation.

Neil had not known any of that. He began paying attention to who was described as aggressive in his warehouse, and why, and found that the pattern was not limited to Desmond. He started asking for specifics every time, and the word intimidating came up much less often after that.
observe: Notice moments of wariness or unease you feel around Black men this week, and what the man was actually doing at the time.
Notice how often you hear Black colleagues or acquaintances described as aggressive, intimidating or as having an attitude, and whether specifics are given.
Notice how Black boys and teenagers are spoken about, and whether they are treated as children.
Notice greetings and conversations among Black men around you, and whether you are reading their energy against your own baseline.

drills.name: Swap Test, Race
steps: Recall a moment when you read a Black man as threatening, aggressive or suspicious.
Write down exactly what he did and said, as a camera would have recorded it.
Imagine the same actions from a white man of the same size in the same place.
Note whether your reading changes, and write a fairer description if it does.
variations: Run the swap test on a positive reading too, such as finding a white man naturally authoritative, and see whether your reading holds for a Black man.
Ask a friend to run the swap test on a story you tell about someone you found intimidating, without telling them your conclusion.
Swap age as well as race, and imagine the same behaviour from a much younger or older man.

drills.name: Ask for Specifics
steps: The next time someone describes a person of colour as aggressive, intimidating or difficult, ask what specifically they said or did.
Listen for whether the answer is about behaviour or about manner and size.
Note how the conversation changes when specifics are asked for.
variations: Ask for specifics when someone describes a person of any background as difficult, and notice whether the answers differ.
Read back a reference or appraisal you have written and check every adjective for the behaviour behind it.
When you describe someone yourself, describe the behaviour first and the judgment second, and notice how often the judgment changes.

drills.name: Act on Behaviour
steps: Choose one setting where you have power to act: a shop, a workplace, a building.
Write down the behaviours that would genuinely justify concern, such as specific actions or words.
Commit to acting only on those, not on unease or how someone looks.
Review after a month whether your actions matched the list.
variations: Share your list of behaviours with the people who work with you, and ask whether anything on it would apply differently to different customers.
Review one decision you made in the past month, such as a complaint, a warning or a refusal, and check it against your list.
Ask a colleague you trust to tell you if they ever see you act on unease rather than behaviour.

drills.name: Check the Age
steps: The next time you see a group of teenagers behaving boisterously, estimate their ages.
Ask yourself whether you would read the same behaviour differently from younger-looking or white teenagers.
Remind yourself that they are children.
Note anything you would do differently as a result.
variations: Look up the age range of the school year groups in your area, so that you have a sense of how young a Year 9 pupil really is.
Notice how teenage boys are described in local news, and whether some are called children and others young men.
When you next see a group of teenagers, guess their age, then look for clues such as uniforms, bags or a parent nearby, and compare.

quiz.q: A friend says our sense of how big and strong someone looks simply reflects how big and strong they are. What did Wilson, Hugenberg and Rule find?
options: He is right, because judgments of size in their studies matched the men's actual measurements
Young Black men were judged larger and stronger than white men of the same actual size
White men were judged larger than Black men, regardless of how big each man actually was
Judgments of size were random and bore no relation to race or to any facial features
quiz.explain: Participants judged Black men larger, stronger and more capable of harm than white men matched for size. The bias was strongest for darker skin and more stereotypically Black features.

quiz.q: What did Goff and colleagues find when students estimated the ages of boys suspected of crimes?
options: Black boys' ages were overestimated by about four and a half years on average
All boys' ages were estimated accurately, whatever their race or the crime
Black boys were judged younger and more innocent than white or Latino boys
Ages were overestimated only for the youngest boys, those under ten years old
quiz.explain: Black boys were seen as about four and a half years older than they were, and as less innocent than other boys from about the age of ten. The protection usually extended to children was withdrawn earlier.

quiz.q: In Payne's 2001 study, what happened when participants had to identify objects quickly after seeing a face?
options: They identified guns and tools equally accurately, whatever the face was
They mistook guns for tools more often after seeing a white face
They mistook tools for guns more often after seeing a Black face
They refused to answer when the face shown to them was a Black face
quiz.explain: Under time pressure, tools were more often mistaken for guns after Black faces. The bias lay in the automatic part of the response, before deliberate control could step in.

quiz.q: In Wilson and colleagues' studies, what did inflated judgments of Black men's size and strength predict?
options: How friendly participants expected the men to be in conversation
How much the participants would trust the men with their money
How tall participants believed themselves to be, compared with the men
How justified participants thought force against the men would be
quiz.explain: Inflated judgments of size and strength predicted how justified participants thought it would be to use force against the men if suspected of a crime. The authors saw this as one possible contributor to unjustified force.

quiz.q: You are alone in a lift when a tall Black man you do not know steps in. You notice a flicker of unease. What fits this chapter best?
options: Stay where you are, ask yourself what he is actually doing, and treat him as you would anyone
Step out at the next floor, since it is always better to be safe than to ignore your instincts
Keep your eyes on him the whole time, so that you are ready if he does anything
Make a joke about the weather, so that he knows you are not prejudiced against him
quiz.explain: The unease is a fast reading, not evidence. Acting on behaviour rather than feeling, and treating him as you would anyone, is what accuracy requires.

quiz.q: A colleague describes a Black co-worker as aggressive and having an attitude. What is the most useful response?
options: Agree, since your colleague works with him every day and knows him better than you
Ask what he actually did, and whether a white colleague would be described the same way
Warn the co-worker that people find him aggressive, so that he can change
Report the co-worker to HR, so that there is a record of the concern
quiz.explain: Asking for specifics separates behaviour from manner and size. The swap test checks whether the same behaviour would be described the same way from someone else.

quiz.q: In Wilson, Hugenberg and Rule's studies, for which men was the inflation of perceived size and strength strongest?
options: For men who were in fact larger and stronger than any of the others photographed
For darker-skinned men with more stereotypically Black features, though no larger
For men who were photographed smiling, compared with men with neutral faces
For white men who were photographed beside Black men of the very same size
quiz.explain: The bias was strongest for men with darker skin and more stereotypically Black facial features, even though those men were no larger. The inflated judgments also predicted how justified force against them seemed.

quiz.q: On a bus, an older passenger feels threatened by four loud Black teenagers at the back, and guesses they are about nineteen. What fits this chapter best?
options: Report them to the driver as a gang causing trouble, since loud groups are a threat
Check the age, run the swap test, and act only on behaviour
Move downstairs and avoid looking at them, since eye contact might provoke them
Tell them to quieten down, since young men respond best to a firm adult voice
quiz.explain: Black boys are often seen as several years older and less innocent than they are. Remembering they may be children, running the swap test and responding only to behaviour that would worry him in anyone gives a fairer reading.

quiz.q: Someone says the best way to avoid racial bias is simply not to see colour. What does this chapter suggest?
options: That the biases that matter work before deliberate thought, so deliberate checks are needed
That not seeing colour fully removes automatic bias in how big or old someone looks
That racial bias only appears in people who openly hold prejudiced views about others
That bias can be removed in a single training session, after which no checks are needed
quiz.explain: Payne found that bias lay in the automatic part of the response. Not seeing colour does not switch it off; noticing where it operates and using checks such as the swap test reduces its effects.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific moment when you read a Black man or boy, or saw others read him, as threatening, aggressive, older or suspicious. Describe what he actually did, as a camera would have recorded it, and what was concluded. Now apply the swap test: would the same behaviour have been read the same way from a white man or boy of the same size and age? Describe one way you will slow down, ask for specifics or act on behaviour rather than unease in future.
reflection.guidance: These readings are fast and largely automatic, and finding one in yourself is not a confession of malice. The aim is to notice where your perception supplies something that was not there, and to act on what people do. Be specific about the moment and about what you will do differently.

failureMode: The first failure is to trust your sense of how big, strong or threatening a Black man is, when research shows such judgments are inflated. The second is to read Black boys as older and less innocent than they are. The third is to act on unease rather than behaviour: following, avoiding, calling security. The fourth is to accept descriptions of Black colleagues as aggressive without asking for specifics. The fifth is to read animated conversation or expressive greetings as conflict, by applying a quieter baseline. And the sixth is to expect Black men to make themselves smaller so that they are read accurately, when the burden of accuracy belongs with the reader.

moreCases.title: The student buying a suit
moreCases.scene:
Jerome, nineteen, is a Black law student, and he has his first interview for a summer placement at a law firm next week. On Saturday he goes to a department store in the city centre to buy his first suit, with money he has saved from his part-time job. He is wearing a hoodie and trainers, and he has his headphones round his neck.

Within a minute of his walking into the menswear department, a security guard has moved from the escalator to a spot near the suits. As Jerome looks through the rails, the guard follows at a distance, stopping whenever he stops. A sales assistant comes over and asks whether she can help him, then stays beside him without saying anything else. When Jerome takes two suits to the fitting room, the guard stands outside the curtain.

Jerome comes out, hangs the suits back on the rail without trying them on, and leaves. He buys a suit the following week at a smaller shop where the owner, an older man, measures him, talks to him about the interview and tells him to come back if he gets the job.

He writes a short, polite complaint to the department store. It reaches the store manager, Sandra, fifty-two, who asks for the CCTV footage and watches the whole twenty minutes.

He had chosen the department store because his mother had bought his father's wedding suit there, thirty years earlier, and had told him it was the place to go for something that mattered.

On the bus home, he looks at the interview invitation on his phone and wonders whether the law firm will see him the same way. He decides to wear the suit from the smaller shop, and to wear it well.

The owner of the smaller shop, when Jerome mentions the department store, nods and says that his own son had the same experience there, twenty years ago.
moreCases.misread:
The security guard and the sales assistant read a young Black man in a hoodie in the suit department as a possible shoplifter, and acted on that reading by following and hovering. Jerome read their behaviour accurately, as suspicion, and left.

The sales assistant, if asked, would probably have said she was being helpful. Staying silent beside someone, without offering help, is how helpfulness turns into surveillance.

The guard read Jerome's leaving without trying the suits on as confirmation that he had been up to something, when it was a young man who had been made to feel like a thief in a place he had chosen for an important purchase.

Sandra's first reading of the complaint, before she watched the footage, had been that a customer was being oversensitive. The footage changed her mind in the first three minutes.
moreCases.betterRead:
Wilson, Hugenberg and Rule found that young Black men were judged larger, stronger and more threatening than white men of the same size, and Payne found that race shaped split-second readings of threat. Unease of that kind feels like perception, and the guard and the assistant acted on it. Sandra, watching the footage, could see that Jerome had done nothing except look at suits. Her better response used the Act on Behaviour drill in this chapter: she wrote down, with her security team, the specific behaviours that would justify attention, such as concealing goods or removing tags, and made clear that staff should act on those and nothing else. She ran the swap test with the guard, asking whether he would have followed a white student in a hoodie. He admitted that he would not. Sandra wrote to Jerome, apologised and invited him back. He did not come back, but he wrote to say that the apology meant something.

Sandra also asked the store's trainer to add the swap test to the induction for all new security and sales staff.

moreCases.title: The boys on the bus
moreCases.scene:
Brian, sixty-six, is on the top deck of a bus on his way home from the hospital, where he has had a long appointment. Four Black teenage boys get on and sit at the back. They are loud: laughing, shouting across the seats at one another, playing music on a phone and pushing each other in play. One of them is tall and broad, and Brian guesses that they are eighteen or nineteen.

Brian feels uneasy. He moves to a seat nearer the stairs. When one of the boys stands up suddenly and lurches down the aisle as the bus brakes, Brian's heart jumps. He goes down to the driver and says that there is a gang of young men upstairs causing trouble.

The driver, a woman in her forties, goes up to have a look. She comes back down after a minute and says, quite gently, that they are kids from the secondary school on the next road, they are fourteen, they are being noisy but not doing any harm, and she has asked them to turn the music down.

When the boys get off at the stop after Brian's, he sees them properly for the first time: school blazers under their coats, one of them carrying a trumpet case. The tall one, laughing, has the face of a child.

He had also, earlier that day, sat in the hospital waiting room beside two white teenage boys in the same school's uniform, who were playing music on a phone and laughing. He had not noticed them at all.

The driver mentions, as she sits back down, that she has a son the same age, at the same school, and that he and his friends are just as loud.

Brian's wife, when he tells her about it that evening, asks him how old their grandson is now. Fourteen, he says, and then goes quiet.
moreCases.misread:
Brian read four loud teenagers as young men, a gang and a threat, and read a boy stumbling as the bus braked as a sudden aggressive movement. He reported trouble that did not exist.

He also read his own fear as a sensible response to danger, which is how bias usually feels from the inside.

The other passengers on the top deck, who had been quietly reading their phones, read the boys as noisy children, which is what they were. Brian's fear had been his alone.
moreCases.betterRead:
Goff and colleagues found that students overestimated the ages of Black boys suspected of crimes by an average of four and a half years, and judged them less innocent than other boys from about the age of ten. Brian's guess of eighteen or nineteen was out by about the same margin, and it changed everything: noise from children became menace from men. The lurch down the aisle was a boy losing his balance when the bus braked. The better reading, which the Check the Age drill in this chapter rehearses, starts by remembering that teenagers are children and asking whether the same noise from a group of white schoolboys would have sent him down the stairs. Brian thought about it all evening. He decided that it would not have, and that if the driver had been less sensible, four fourteen-year-olds might have been met at the next stop by the police.

He also told his grandson about it, who is fourteen too, and who said that the same thing happened to his Black friends all the time.

moreCases.title: The greeting across the street
moreCases.scene:
Duncan, fifty-five, runs a café on a high street with a barbershop opposite. One Saturday morning, he is setting out the tables on the pavement when a car pulls up and a young Black man, Isaac, gets out and shouts across the street to another, Tunde, who is coming out of the barbershop. Tunde shouts back, louder. They stride towards each other in the middle of the road, arms out, still shouting. Isaac grabs Tunde's hand, pulls him into a hard hug and thumps him on the back, and both of them are laughing and talking over each other at full volume.

For the first few seconds, Duncan reads it as the start of a fight. He has his phone out and his thumb over the emergency number before he understands what he is seeing. His teenage daughter, Ella, who is helping him, laughs and says, "Dad, they're mates." Isaac has just come back from a year working abroad.

Duncan puts his phone away, embarrassed. The two men come into the café twenty minutes later, still talking loudly, and order breakfast. They are friendly, funny and tip well.

That evening, Duncan thinks about how close he came to making a call, and about what might have happened next if he had.

Ella also tells him that Tunde is the barber who cut her friend's brother's hair for his school prom, and that he is lovely.

Duncan has lived in the area for twenty years, and the barbershop opened three years ago. He realises he has never once spoken to the barber, though they open their shutters at the same time every morning.

He also remembers that he had, without thinking, stepped back towards the café door as the two men strode towards each other, as if to put the tables between himself and them.
moreCases.misread:
Duncan read two Black men shouting and striding towards each other as the beginning of a fight, and very nearly called the police. He was applying a quieter baseline to a greeting that, within their circle, meant warmth and joy.

And he read the volume as the important signal, when the laughter, the open arms and the hug were all telling him something else.

His thumb on the phone was the reading made into an action, and an action of that kind cannot easily be taken back once the call is made.
moreCases.betterRead:
This chapter describes greetings among many Black men as expressive and physical: the dap, the pull-in hug, the call across a room. Part III described the history of the dap. Within those communities, the behaviour is read accurately as affection. Misreading happens when outsiders apply a quieter baseline, so that a loud greeting becomes aggression. Payne's work suggests that such readings are made in fractions of a second, and are shaped by race before deliberate thought arrives. Duncan's better reading, which his daughter supplied, was the one this book recommends everywhere: look for more than one signal, and wait a second before acting. The laughter, the open arms and the hug were all there. He also noticed, when he ran the swap test, that two white men greeting each other the same way after a year apart would probably have made him smile.

Duncan told the story to a friend, who admitted that he had once called the police on a group of young Black men in a park who had turned out to be a church youth group.

moreCases.title: The man at the window
moreCases.scene:
Malik, thirty, is a nurse, and he has lived on a quiet street of terraced houses for two years. One night, after a twelve-hour shift, he gets home at eleven to find that he has left his keys at work. His flatmate is away. He goes round to the back of the house, where the kitchen window is open a crack, and starts trying to push it up and climb in.

His neighbour across the back alley, Peter, fifty-eight, hears the noise and looks out of his bedroom window. He sees a tall Black man in a dark coat climbing through a window. He does not recognise him in the dark. His hand goes to his phone.

Then he hesitates. He remembers something his son said to him once, about how often men like Malik have the police called on them for being in their own homes. He asks himself what he would do if he saw a white man climbing in, and realises that he would probably open his window and call out to ask whether everything was all right.

So he does. "Everything OK over there?" Malik, half through the window, says that he has locked himself out, and introduces himself. Peter says he has seen him going to work in his uniform, and asks whether he needs a hand.

Malik has had the police called on him once before, two years earlier, when he was waiting in his car outside a friend's house. He has not forgotten it, and as Peter's window opens, his whole body tenses.

In the brief silence before Peter speaks, Malik keeps his hands where they can be seen on the window frame, as he was taught to as a teenager, and waits.
moreCases.misread:
Peter's first reading was of a stranger, large and threatening, breaking into a house, and his first impulse was to call the police. The same behaviour from a white man, he realised, would have prompted a question rather than a call.

Malik, for his part, read the opening window as the start of something dangerous, because experience had taught him to.

Peter's hesitation came from a single memory of his son's words, which shows how much a small piece of knowledge can change what a person does in the next five seconds.
moreCases.betterRead:
Wilson and colleagues found that inflated judgments of Black men's size and strength predicted how justified people thought force would be against them, and Payne found that threat is read faster and more readily after seeing a Black face. A tall Black man climbing through a window at night is exactly the kind of ambiguous scene in which those biases do their work. Peter did not ignore the situation; he responded to the behaviour with a question he would have asked anyone, which is what the swap test is for. If Malik had not been able to answer, or had run, Peter could still have called for help. Asking first cost nothing and avoided a call that could have put his neighbour in danger in his own home. Peter came round with a stepladder, and Malik climbed in safely. They have said hello every morning since.

Malik said later that Peter's question was the first time a neighbour had ever asked him whether he was all right rather than what he was doing.

workedReading.title: Handling a report that a boy was aggressive
workedReading.scene:
Anita, forty-four, is head of year at a large secondary school. On a Wednesday afternoon, she receives a written incident report from a supply teacher about Tyrone, fourteen, a Black boy in Year 9. It says that Tyrone was "aggressive and intimidating" in a science lesson, that he "squared up" to the teacher, and that the teacher felt threatened. The report asks for a fixed-term exclusion. Anita knows Tyrone a little: he is tall for his age, quiet in most lessons, and on the school's football team. She also knows the research described in this chapter, and the school's own figures, which show that Black boys are excluded at a higher rate than their classmates. She decides not to act on the report until she has done the checks this chapter describes.

She has also read the three earlier reports in Tyrone's file before, and accepted them without question. She notices that she had not, at the time, asked what he had actually done.

She also remembers a conversation with Tyrone's mother at a parents' evening the year before, in which his mother said that she worried every day about how teachers saw her son, and Anita had told her not to worry.

She is also aware that Tyrone's family has been at the school for years, and that his older brother left at sixteen after an exclusion that, she now wonders, may have rested on reports like this one.

steps.label: Check the age
steps.text:
Before anything else, she reminds herself that Tyrone is fourteen. Goff and colleagues found that people overestimate the ages of Black boys by an average of four and a half years, so that a fourteen-year-old may be seen as a young man of eighteen or more. The report's language, "squared up", "intimidating", reads like a description of an adult. She resolves to judge what happened as the behaviour of a child.

She also notices that she had, reading the report, pictured an older, larger boy than Tyrone is, before she reminded herself of his age.

She also looks at the school photograph on his file, which shows a boy with a round face and a nervous smile, to anchor the report in the child it describes.

steps.label: Ask for specifics
steps.text:
She meets the supply teacher and asks him to describe exactly what Tyrone said and did, as a camera would have recorded it. He says that he told Tyrone to move seats, Tyrone stood up, said "Why me? I haven't done anything," and stood by his desk without moving. When asked what "squared up" meant, the teacher says that Tyrone stood up straight and looked at him. Tyrone did not move towards him or raise a hand.

She also asks whether any other pupils were involved, and learns that the two boys who had been talking were not asked to move.

She also asks the teacher how he was feeling that afternoon. He admits that it was his first day at the school, and that he had been warned that Year 9 could be difficult.

steps.label: Run the swap test
steps.text:
She asks herself, and later the teacher, whether a white boy of the same size who stood up, protested and stood still would have been described as squaring up. The teacher, to his credit, thinks about it and says he is not sure. Anita writes down the behaviour without the adjectives: stood up, protested, did not move seats when asked, did not move towards the teacher.

She also asks herself whether she would have reached for the word "intimidating" if she had only read the bare behaviour, and concludes that she would not.

steps.label: Hear his account
steps.text:
She talks to Tyrone, with his form tutor present. He is guarded at first, looking at the floor. When she asks what happened, he says that two other boys had been talking, the teacher had picked on him, and he had stood up because he was angry about being blamed. He says that teachers often think he is threatening because he is big, and that he has learned to keep his hands by his sides. Anita listens without interrupting.

She also notices that Tyrone's account matches the teacher's on every point of behaviour. They differ only on what it meant.

She also notices that he says he stood up because he was angry, which is an honest account of a feeling that any fourteen-year-old blamed in front of the class might have.

steps.label: Look at the pattern
steps.text:
She checks Tyrone's record. There are three previous incidents, all described with similar words, "intimidating", "aggressive manner", "threatening body language", and none describing any physical act. She also checks how often those words appear in reports about other boys in the year group, and notices that they cluster around a small number of Black boys.

She takes the pattern to the senior leadership team, with the reports anonymised, so that the conversation is about the school's language rather than about any one teacher.

She also notes that the reports came from four different teachers, which tells her that the pattern is in the school's habits of description, not in one person.

steps.label: Decide on behaviour
steps.text:
She decides that Tyrone's refusal to move seats was a breach of the school's rules and deserves the usual consequence, a short detention, as it would for any pupil. She decides that nothing in his behaviour justifies an exclusion or the word "intimidating". She explains her reasoning to the supply teacher and to Tyrone's mother, and records the incident in behavioural terms only.

She also tells Tyrone directly that standing up and protesting was not the right way to handle being blamed, and talks with him about what he could do next time, as she would with any pupil.

steps.label: What happened
steps.text:
Tyrone serves the detention without complaint. His mother tells Anita that it is the first time a teacher has taken his side of a story seriously. Anita raises the pattern of language in incident reports at the next staff meeting, and the school changes its reporting form so that staff must describe what a pupil said and did before giving any judgment. Over the following year, the number of reports using "intimidating" falls sharply.

She also writes to the supply agency, without blame, to suggest that its teachers be given the school's guidance on describing behaviour before they start.

She also tells Tyrone's mother, a year later at another parents' evening, that she was right to worry, and that the school has tried to change.

moreFailures.title: Praising a Black man for not fitting the stereotype
moreFailures.body:
Comments such as "You're so articulate," "You're not what I expected," "You're one of the good ones" or "You don't seem threatening at all" are usually meant as compliments. They land as something else. Each one reveals the stereotype the speaker started with and tells the man that he has been measured against it and has passed, this time. They also imply that the ordinary qualities they praise, speaking well, being gentle, being professional, are surprising in a Black man, which is the stereotype restated. Many Black men describe hearing such comments throughout their lives, and the cumulative effect can be wearing. If you want to praise someone, praise something specific that they did: the clarity of their argument in a meeting, the care they took with a client, the goal they scored. Leave out the comparison with what you expected.

A good check is to ask whether you would say the same thing to a white colleague who did the same thing.

Many Black men can recite the comments they have heard most often. Most of them were meant as praise.

moreFailures.title: Saying you do not see colour
moreFailures.body:
Many people respond to discussions of racial bias by saying that they do not see colour and treat everyone the same. It is usually sincere, and it reflects a real wish to be fair. But the research in this chapter suggests that the biases that matter most operate before deliberate thought: in how big a man looks, how old a boy seems, how quickly a tool becomes a gun. Payne found that the bias lay in the automatic part of the response. Not seeing colour does not switch those processes off; it only makes it harder to notice them and to use the checks that reduce their effects, such as the swap test, asking for specifics and checking the age. Fairness, in practice, comes from noticing where bias is likely to operate and slowing down there, not from believing that you are immune to it.

The aim is not to see colour constantly, but to notice it in the moments where it is likely to bend your judgment.

moreFailures.title: Making one man the spokesperson
moreFailures.body:
When race comes up at work, in a training session, a discussion of the news or a review of policy, it is common for people to turn to the one Black man in the room and ask what he thinks, or how Black people feel about it, or whether something is racist. It can feel like inclusion. To many Black men it feels like being put on display, made to represent a whole group, and asked to do the work of educating colleagues, often while managing their own reaction to the topic. Some may welcome the chance to speak; many will not, and the request puts them in a difficult position either way. If you want to hear his view, ask privately, as you would ask anyone about anything personal, and accept a no. Do your own reading. And when changes are being made, ask who is doing the work, and whether it is fairly shared.

If a Black colleague chooses to speak, listen to him as one person with one view, not as a representative.

moreFailures.title: Dismissing the caution Black men carry
moreFailures.body:
Many Black men describe habits learned early, often through what is called the talk: hands visible, no sudden movements, no hands in pockets in shops, no running, no arguing with police. Some soften their presence deliberately, smiling more, speaking more quietly, dressing more formally. When they mention these habits, a common response is disbelief or reassurance: "Surely not round here," "You're overthinking it," "I've never seen anything like that." The previous chapter described how questioning someone's map of safety tells them their reading of their own life is wrong. The research in this chapter suggests their caution has reasons. Listen, believe them, and ask what you could do in the places you influence, such as your shop, your workplace or your street, so that the caution becomes a little less necessary there.

It also helps to remember that the caution is usually invisible when it works, which is why it is so easy to doubt.

If he asks you to back him up, for example by speaking to a manager about how he has been described, do it.

questions.q: If these biases are automatic, can I do anything about them?
questions.a:
Yes, though not by deciding to be unbiased. The research suggests the biases operate fast and largely outside awareness, so the useful steps are about behaviour rather than feeling. Notice the moments where they are most likely to operate: under time pressure, in ambiguous situations, when you are tired or stressed, and when the man is a stranger. Slow down there before acting. Use the swap test, imagining the same behaviour from a white man of the same size. Ask for specifics when anyone, including you, describes a Black man as aggressive or intimidating. Remember that boys are children. Look for evidence that would disconfirm your reading. And act only on behaviour that would justify the same action from anyone, as Sandra's store and Anita's school both did.

It also helps to know that the checks feel awkward at first and become quicker with practice.

And when you get it wrong, which everyone sometimes does, apologise simply and change what you do.

questions.q: Isn't it just that some men are genuinely more intimidating?
questions.a:
Some people are genuinely threatening, and behaviour that would worry you in anyone should worry you here. But the question is whether your sense of how intimidating someone is matches what they are doing. Wilson, Hugenberg and Rule found that participants judged Black men larger, stronger and more capable of harm than white men of exactly the same size, with the bias strongest for darker-skinned men who were no larger. That means part of what feels like an accurate perception is added by the perceiver. The practical test is to ask what the person actually did and said, as Neil did with Desmond's complainants and Anita did with the supply teacher. If the answer is about size, a serious face or a firm voice rather than behaviour, the intimidation may be in the reading.

A useful follow-up is to ask the person describing the intimidation whether they would use the same word about anyone else who did the same thing.

questions.q: What should I do if I feel uneasy around a Black man in a public place?
questions.a:
Notice the unease, and do not act on it unless there is behaviour that would justify acting with anyone. Stay where you are in the lift; do not cross the road ostentatiously; do not follow him round the shop or call security because of how he looks. Each of these actions is noticed and remembered, and each tells the man that he has been read as a threat for being there. Ask yourself whether you would feel the same unease with a white man of the same size, dressed the same way, doing the same thing. If you would not, the feeling is information about the bias rather than about him. If someone's behaviour is genuinely threatening, respond to the behaviour, as you would with anyone, and get help if you need it.

It also helps to remember that he may well have noticed your unease before you did, and is managing it too.

And if you have reacted on unease before, the next time is a chance to do it differently.

questions.q: How can I support Black colleagues without making it awkward?
questions.a:
Mostly through what you do when others are reading them. When someone describes a Black colleague as aggressive, intimidating or having an attitude, ask what specifically he said or did, as this chapter's Ask for Specifics drill suggests. When his idea passes without comment and is later praised from someone else, credit it to him, as Part IV's chapter on the glass ceiling described. Do not make him the spokesperson on race, and do not praise him for not fitting a stereotype. Treat his directness, his expressiveness or his reserve as you would anyone's. If he tells you about his experience of being read, listen and believe him. And if you have power over decisions about pay, promotion or discipline, check whether descriptions of Black staff are based on behaviour or on manner.

It can also help to ask Black colleagues, privately and without pressure, whether there is anything about the workplace they would change.

questions.q: Why do some Black men seem guarded or formal in mixed settings?
questions.a:
For many, it is a response to being read. This chapter describes how many Black men grow up with a constant awareness of how their bodies are interpreted, and learn to manage it: keeping their voices low, their hands visible, their faces neutral, their dress formal. Desmond told Neil that he did this without thinking. It is a form of the vigilance described in the previous chapter and the masking described earlier in this part, and a later chapter looks at code-switching. From outside, it can look like coldness or reserve. It is not yours to dismantle, and it is not a sign that something is wrong with the man. The useful response is to make the setting one where such care is less necessary, and to treat whatever he chooses to show with ordinary respect.

If he relaxes over time in your company, take it as a sign that the setting has become safer, not as a reward you have earned.

It is also worth noticing how much effort that care takes, and that it is effort others do not have to spend.

questions.q: Does this research apply to other groups too?
questions.a:
The studies in this chapter mostly concern Black men in the United States, and their findings should not be stretched too far. But similar patterns of misreading have been described for other racialised groups in other places: young men from particular backgrounds being followed in shops, described as aggressive at work or treated as older than they are. The methods for reading fairly travel well, whatever the group: check the age, ask for specifics, run the swap test, act only on behaviour that would justify the same action from anyone, and look for evidence that would disconfirm your reading. The deeper principle of this book applies everywhere: the burden of accuracy belongs to the reader, not to the person being read.

It is also worth reading accounts written by people from the groups concerned, which often say more than the research can.

It also helps to ask people from the groups concerned what they would most like others to know, and to take their answers seriously.

watch.notice: A father teaches his children what to do if stopped by police, and later a routine stop turns fatal. Notice the instructions about hands, movement and voice, and how carefully the young man is taught to manage how his body will be read.

watch.notice: The story of five teenagers wrongly convicted in New York in 1989. Notice how young they look, and how differently they were seen and described at the time, the pattern Goff and colleagues later measured.
